## This week’s sociological question

<div class="chapter-question">When an LLM drafts experimental material, how do we know that the candidates vary the intended construct rather than several things at once?</div>

## Connection to the preceding material

Week 4 examined how an unfolding situation becomes evidence. Week 5 examines the other side of the research encounter: how sociologists construct a situation, vignette, message or profile so that a comparison can support a causal claim.

## Learning outcomes

You should be able to distinguish a vignette, audit study, confederate design and field experiment; explain factorial survey logic; identify semantic differences that act as treatment confounds; distinguish a generated candidate population from a validated treatment set; and explain what an embedding-and-UMAP map can and cannot establish.

## Essential readings and what each contributes

::: {.reading-list}
- **Methods:** Wallander (2009), “25 Years of Factorial Surveys in Sociology,” *Social Science Research* 38(3): 505–520. Read the complete article. It establishes how sociologists combine experimentally varied vignette dimensions. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ssresearch.2009.03.004). [@Wallander2009]
- **AI-assisted experiment:** Bai et al. (2025), “LLM-Generated Messages Can Persuade Humans on Policy Issues,” *Nature Communications* 16: 6037. Read the complete article. It compares human-written, LLM-generated and human-selected LLM messages in experiments with human participants. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-61345-5). [@BaiEtAl2025]
- **Substantive application:** Bloemraad, Silva and Voss (2016), “Rights, Economics, or Family?” *Social Forces* 94(4): 1647–1674. Read the complete article. It tests competing frames in an immigration-policy experiment and supplies the substantive case used in the lecture. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1093/sf/sov123). [@BloemraadSilvaVoss2016]
:::

## Additional readings grouped by purpose

- **For treatment wording and non-focal information:** Dafoe, Zhang and Caughey (2018), “Information Equivalence in Survey Experiments,” *Political Analysis* 26(4): 399–416. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2018.9). [@DafoeZhangCaughey2018]
- **For adaptive instruments:** Velez (2025), “Crowdsourced Adaptive Surveys,” *Political Analysis*. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2024.34). [@Velez2025]

## Sociological and methodological background

Sociologists intervene in several ways. A vignette describes a situation and asks for a judgment; a factorial survey varies several attributes across vignettes; an audit study sends matched applications that differ on a focal signal; a confederate enacts a standardized role in a social setting. The concrete objects differ, but each design depends on controlling which feature changes and what comparison that change licenses.

Wallander’s review matters because generated text does not make this design logic obsolete. An LLM can produce a larger candidate pool, but every candidate still embeds word choice, tone, plausibility and social assumptions. If one immigration frame invokes “human dignity” and another makes an unsupported claim about public costs, the conditions differ in more than a short label. Those semantic differences are potential confounds.

## Synthesis of the current LLM literature

Bai and colleagues provide the central AI-assisted experiment for this week. They compare messages written by people, messages generated by an LLM and LLM messages selected by people before testing those materials with human participants. Their design lets us study a production procedure, but it does not make every output from that procedure a valid treatment. Dafoe and colleagues offer a useful standard for reviewing the resulting texts: non-focal information should remain comparable across conditions. The coding exercise therefore generates a population of 60 messages and uses embeddings and UMAP to choose cases for closer reading. Velez extends the problem by allowing participant responses to change the question bank while a survey is running.

## Summary and preparation for next week

Generation expands a design space. It does not decide which distinctions are causal, plausible or ethical. Week 6 makes the treatment path dynamic: the model chooses or composes the next question after seeing a participant’s answer.
